title: Old vs New Tax Regime
tagline: India lets you choose how you're taxed. The New regime: low rates, almost no deductions. The Old regime: higher rates, but rewards saving and renting. How to know which one wins for you.
summary: The two income-tax regimes, the FY2025-26 slabs, and how to choose between them.

paragraphs: Since FY 2020-21 India has had **two income-tax regimes**, and you can pick the one that costs you less. The **New regime** (now the default) offers lower tax rates but strips away almost all deductions and exemptions. The **Old regime** keeps higher rates but lets you reduce your taxable income through deductions like 80C, HRA, and home-loan interest.
The trade is simple to state: the New regime rewards *not* needing deductions; the Old regime rewards *using* lots of them.

blocks.title: First, the good news for Aarav
blocks.text: Aarav earns ₹20,000/month = ₹2.4 lakh a year. That's below the taxable limit in BOTH regimes, so right now he pays ZERO income tax. This module is about his future self — the day his salary crosses the tax thresholds — so he chooses correctly from day one.

blocks.title: New regime (default) — standard deduction ₹75,000 for salaried
The ₹12 lakh headline
blocks.text: Under the New regime, a Section 87A rebate (up to ₹60,000) makes taxable income up to ₹12 lakh effectively tax-free. With the ₹75,000 standard deduction, a salaried person earning up to ~₹12.75 lakh gross can pay zero tax — without claiming a single deduction.

blocks.title: Old regime — standard deduction ₹50,000; deductions allowed
blocks.caption: Old-regime 87A rebate makes income up to ₹5 lakh tax-free; deductions (80C, HRA, etc.) reduce taxable income first.

paragraphs: The Old regime only wins if your **total deductions are large enough** to push your taxable income below what the New regime's lower rates would tax. The big Old-regime levers are: **80C** (up to ₹1.5 lakh — EPF, PPF, ELSS, life insurance, etc.), **HRA** (if you pay rent), **home-loan interest** (up to ₹2 lakh under Sec 24b), **80D** (health insurance), and **80CCD(1B)** (extra ₹50,000 for NPS).

items.detail: you have few deductions — you don't pay much rent, have no home loan, and don't invest heavily in 80C instruments. True for most young earners early in their careers.
you stack big deductions — high HRA in a metro, a home-loan interest of ₹2 lakh, a full ₹1.5 lakh 80C, ₹50k NPS, plus 80D. Together these can outweigh the New regime's lower rates.

Don't guess. Compute your tax both ways (any online calculator or your payroll portal does this) for your actual deductions, and pick the lower number. Re-check whenever your rent, loan, or investments change.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Never choose a tax regime by reputation — choose it by arithmetic. For a young person with simple finances, the New regime is usually both simpler and cheaper. Crucially: don't buy a product you don't want (like a dud insurance policy) just to claim an Old-regime deduction — the tax saved rarely beats the bad investment's cost.

cheatsheet: India has two regimes; you pick the cheaper one. New is the default.
New regime: lower rates, almost no deductions; 87A rebate makes taxable income up to ₹12L tax-free (≈₹12.75L gross salary with the ₹75k standard deduction).
Old regime: higher rates but allows 80C (₹1.5L), HRA, home-loan interest (₹2L), 80D, NPS (₹50k); 87A covers income up to ₹5L.
Old wins only if your total deductions are large enough to beat the New regime's lower rates.
Aarav at ₹2.4L/yr pays zero tax in both — this matters for his higher-earning future.
Choose by arithmetic, not reputation; never buy a bad product just to grab a deduction.

questions.prompt: Future Aarav earns ₹13 lakh and has almost no deductions (rents cheaply, no home loan, minimal 80C). Which regime is likely better, and why?
questions.hint: The Old regime's advantage comes from deductions he doesn't have.
answer: The **New regime** is almost certainly better. Its whole disadvantage is losing deductions — but Aarav barely has any, so he gives up little while gaining the lower rates and the generous 87A/standard-deduction structure. The Old regime would tax him at higher rates with no large deductions to offset them.

The Old regime only pays off when someone stacks big deductions (high HRA, ₹2 lakh home-loan interest, full 80C, NPS, 80D). With a near-empty deduction sheet, the New regime wins on both simplicity and cost. He should still confirm with a quick both-ways calculation.
keyPoints: New regime wins with few deductions
Old regime needs big deductions to beat lower New rates
Aarav has little to deduct → New
Always verify with a both-ways calculation

questions.prompt: An agent tells Aarav: 'Buy this ₹50,000/year insurance policy — you'll save tax under 80C!' Why is this often bad advice?
questions.hint: Compare the tax saved to the quality of the underlying product, and which regime he's on.
answer: Two problems. First, 80C deductions only help under the **Old regime** — if Aarav is on the New regime (likely, given few deductions), the policy saves him no tax at all. Second, even under the Old regime, the **tax saved is a fraction of the premium** (e.g. 20–30% of ₹50,000), while many such 'tax-saving' insurance-cum-investment policies are poor investments with high costs and weak returns. You'd be spending ₹50,000 on a bad product to save ₹10,000–15,000 in tax.
The principle: never let the tax tail wag the investment dog. Buy term insurance for protection and invest separately in low-cost funds; choose your regime by the maths, not by an agent's commission.
keyPoints: 80C only helps in the Old regime
Many tax-saving policies are poor investments
Don't buy bad products for a deduction
Tax shouldn't drive the investment decision
